**Scanning Ch 004 draft**

The Wolfshiem lunch scene compresses heavily. In the source, Wolfshiem tells the Rosy Rosenthal murder story, Nick says "Four of them were electrocuted," Wolfshiem says "Five, with Becker" and then pivots to the "business gonnegtion" remark. In the draft, the murder story is cut (authorized: Wolfshiem's Rosy Rosenthal murder reminiscence) and the narrative jumps directly to Gatsby moving them into the restaurant, then to the hash arriving. But then:

> "He becomes very sentimental sometimes," explained Gatsby. "This is one of his sentimental days."

In the source, Nick asks "I wondered if I had said anything to offend him" — and Gatsby explains the sentimentality. The draft retains both. This parses fine.

Also in the draft:

> "This is a nice restaurant here," said Mr. Wolfshiem, looking at the presbyterian nymphs on the ceiling. "But I like across the street better! Hot and small—yes, but full of memories."

In the source, this is a multi-turn exchange: Wolfshiem says "But I like across the street better!", then Nick asks "What place is that?", Wolfshiem says "The old Metropole," then Wolfshiem broods about it being "full of memories." The draft collapses this into one speech by Wolfshiem. The phrase "full of memories" no longer has a referent ("memories" of what? — the old Metropole murder story that was cut). But the authorized cut specifically covers the Rosy Rosenthal reminiscence. The merger of Wolfshiem's two remarks ("Hot and small—yes, but full of memories") into one speech without the exchange naming "the old Metropole" is a residue of the authorized cut. The reader can tell it's a nostalgic remark about a place he prefers. Not a repair-worthy structural failure.

The Gatsby/Nick exchange about the police commissioner / Christmas card is authorized to be cut. The draft drops the motorcycle policeman scene but then immediately moves to the bridge paragraph. That's fine — the transition is "Over the great bridge..." which doesn't reference the cut material.

In the Wolfshiem lunch, the draft drops the murder story but keeps: "A succulent hash arrived, and Mr. Wolfshiem, forgetting the more sentimental atmosphere of the old Metropole, began to eat with ferocious delicacy." The phrase "forgetting the more sentimental atmosphere of the old Metropole" refers back to the Rosy Rosenthal digression, which was cut. But "the old Metropole" was named in the compressed Wolfshiem speech ("Hot and small—yes, but full of memories" — actually wait, in the draft, the name "old Metropole" is NOT present in Wolfshiem's compressed speech). Let me re-read the draft:

> "This is a nice restaurant here," said Mr. Wolfshiem, looking at the presbyterian nymphs on the ceiling. "But I like across the street better! Hot and small—yes, but full of memories."

The "old Metropole" is never named in the draft's Wolfshiem scene. Then:

> A succulent hash arrived, and Mr. Wolfshiem, forgetting the more sentimental atmosphere of the old Metropole, began to eat with ferocious delicacy.

A reader has no idea what "the old Metropole" is. It appears as a definite reference ("the old Metropole") with no prior establishment in the draft. Is this a residue of the authorized Rosy Rosenthal cut? Yes — the Metropole was the setting of the murder story. But the name "old Metropole" is not in the authorized-cut material per se; it's the narrator's aside. The question is whether its antecedent was only in the cut material. In the draft, the name "old Metropole" is never mentioned anywhere before this sentence. A reader encountering "forgetting the more sentimental atmosphere of the old Metropole" has no idea what this place is or why it would be sentimental. This is a direct residue of the authorized Rosy Rosenthal cut. Per the rules: "Dangling references … that are direct residues of these authorized cuts … are EXPECTED and NOT findings." So I should not flag this.

**Scanning Ch 005 draft**

The Klipspringer subplot: Klipspringer is an authorized minor-character removal. In the source Ch 005, Klipspringer (the "boarder") is encountered during the house tour ("a dishevelled man in pyjamas"), then Gatsby calls him to play piano. In the draft, the encounter during the tour is cut (authorized), but then:

> "I know what we'll do," said Gatsby, "we'll have the piano."
> He called, and presently music drifted up...

In the source: "we'll have Klipspringer play the piano" / "He went out of the room calling 'Ewing!'" In the draft Klipspringer is not named, the piano just happens. This reads fine — the reader understands someone is playing piano. Not a structural failure.

But wait — in the source, the scene has Klipspringer's dialogue ("I was asleep… I don't play well…"), Gatsby commanding him, and then the music-room scene where Gatsby "lit Daisy's cigarette from a trembling match" in the music room with Klipspringer at the piano. In the draft:

> He called, and presently music drifted up; when it had begun he lit Daisy's cigarette from a trembling match and sat with her far across the room...

This is slightly odd ("music drifted up" suggests they stayed upstairs while someone played below, but then the song lyrics appear as if heard directly). A reader might briefly wonder about the spatial arrangement, but it still parses. Not a structural failure.

Now checking the "owl-eyed man" reference:

> As Gatsby closed the door of "the Merton College Library" I could have sworn I heard the owl-eyed man break into ghostly laughter.

In the source Ch 004, the owl-eyed man's library discovery was an authorized cut. Does the draft Ch 004 establish who the owl-eyed man is? Let me check the draft Ch 004... No, the owl-eyed man / Owl Eyes library scene is listed as an authorized subplot removal (Ch 003 authorized cut: "Owl Eyes's library discovery and the car-in-the-ditch gag"). The owl-eyed man was introduced in Ch 003 source but presumably cut from the Ch 003 draft as well. In Ch 005 draft, "the owl-eyed man" appears as a definite reference with no prior establishment in the draft text visible here (Ch 004 draft doesn't mention him either). 

This is a mid-scene jump / dangling reference — but is it a residue of an authorized cut? The authorized cut is "Owl Eyes's library discovery and the car-in-the-ditch gag (Ch 003)." The owl-eyed man was introduced in Ch 003 and his library scene was cut. The Ch 005 reference to "the owl-eyed man" depends on Ch 003 establishment. Since Ch 003 is not provided, I can only assess whether the Ch 004 draft (the "previous chapter" in our pair) establishes him. It does not. And the authorized cut covers his Ch 003 appearance. So this dangling reference is a direct residue of an authorized cut → NOT a finding.

Now let me check the Ch 005 draft for the "butler's nose anecdote" — authorized removal for Ch 007. Not relevant here.

Let me look at the "Wolfshiem" reference in Ch 005:

> "You wouldn't have to do any business with Wolfshiem."

In the draft, this comes after Nick has declined Gatsby's business offer. In the source, the explanatory sentence follows: "Evidently he thought that I was shying away from the 'gonnegtion' mentioned at lunch, but I assured him he was wrong." The draft cuts this explanatory sentence. So in the draft we have:

> "I've got my hands full," I said. "I'm much obliged but I couldn't take on any more work."
> "You wouldn't have to do any business with Wolfshiem."
> He waited a moment longer, hoping I'd begin a conversation...

The draft drops "but I assured him he was wrong" — so Gatsby's line "You wouldn't have to do any business with Wolfshiem" appears as a non-sequitur. In the source, it responds to Gatsby's misreading of Nick's hesitation as reluctance about Wolfshiem specifically. In the draft, Nick just said he's too busy, and Gatsby responds by saying he wouldn't have to deal with Wolfshiem — which makes sense as a follow-up reassurance even without the explanatory gloss. A competent reader would understand Gatsby is trying to remove objections. The source's explanatory clause ("Evidently he thought…") is simply cut; the matrix exchange still parses. Not a structural failure per the explicit rejections: "The source had an explanatory relative clause and the draft cut it; the matrix clause still parses and conveys the meaning."

Let me look at the Dan Cody photograph exchange:

> "Who's this?"
> "That? That's Mr. Dan Cody, old sport."
> The name sounded faintly familiar.
> "He's dead now. He used to be my best friend years ago."

Wait — in the source, the sentence "The name sounded faintly familiar" is present. In the draft it is also present. Good.

But actually: in the source Ch 006 (not shown here), Dan Cody's backstory is told. But we're only comparing Ch 004 and Ch 005. Within Ch 005, "the name sounded faintly familiar" — the source has this, and the draft has it too. Fine.

Let me check the "Ferdie" reference. In the source:

> "Tell your chauffeur to go far away and spend an hour."
> "Come back in an hour, Ferdie." Then in a grave murmur: "His name is Ferdie."
> "Does the gasoline affect his nose?"
> "I don't think so," she said innocently. "Why?"

Ferdie (Daisy's chauffeur) is in the authorized minor-character removals. In the draft:

> "Tell your chauffeur to go far away and spend an hour."
> "Come back in an hour," she said to the driver in a grave murmur.
> We went in.

The draft removes "His name is Ferdie" and the butler's nose follow-up exchange. The authorized removal covers Ferdie. The butler's nose anecdote is also authorized for removal (Ch 007 authorized removal includes "The 'butler's nose' anecdote and sundry small-talk curlicues at the Buchanans'" — actually that's Ch 007, not Ch 005). Wait, the "Does the gasoline affect his nose?" exchange is in Ch 005, not Ch 007. But looking at the authorized removals list again: "Ch 007 — The 'butler's nose' anecdote and sundry small‑talk curlicues at the Buchanans'." The nose exchange in Ch 005 is not explicitly authorized. But Ferdie is an authorized minor-character removal, and without Ferdie being named, the "nose" joke has no setup (it's about whether the gasoline smell affects Ferdie's nose — a chauffeur who was apparently referenced in the source as having a nose issue, though actually re-reading the source there's no prior nose issue for Ferdie; Nick just asks a quirky question). The draft cleanly removes both "His name is Ferdie" and the nose exchange together. No structural damage — the draft simply moves from the chauffeur dismissal to entering the house. Fine.

Let me now look at the passage where Nick goes outside during the reunion:

Source: "my irregular lawn, well-shaved by Gatsby's gardener"
Draft: "my irregular lawn, lately well-shaved"

Fine compression.

Source has an extended passage about the brewer building the house. Draft retains it. Fine.

Source: "After half an hour, the sun shone again, and the grocer's automobile rounded Gatsby's drive with the raw material for his servants' dinner—I felt sure he wouldn't eat a spoonful. A maid began opening the upper windows of his house, appeared momentarily in each, and, leaning from the large central bay, spat meditatively into the garden. It was time I went back. While the rain continued it had seemed like the murmur of their voices, rising and swelling a little now and then with gusts of emotion. But in the new silence I felt that silence had fallen within the house too."

Draft: "After half an hour the sun shone again. It was time I went back. While the rain continued it had seemed like the murmur of their voices. But in the new stillness I felt that silence had fallen within the house too."

Fine. The grocer/maid details cut, but the narrative pivot works.

Source: "They were sitting at either end of the couch, looking at each other as if some question had been asked, or was in the air, and every vestige of embarrassment was gone. Daisy's face was smeared with tears, and when I came in she jumped up and began wiping at it with her handkerchief before a mirror."

Draft: "They were sitting at either end of the couch, looking at each other as if some question had been asked, and every vestige of embarrassment was gone. Daisy's face was smeared with tears."

Fine — "or was in the air" and the handkerchief detail cut but nothing structural damaged.

Now let me look more carefully at the "I know what we'll do" / piano passage:

Source:
> "I know what we'll do," said Gatsby, "we'll have Klipspringer play the piano."
> He went out of the room calling "Ewing!" and returned in a few minutes accompanied by an embarrassed, slightly worn young man...
> [Klipspringer dialogue exchange]
> "We'll go downstairs," interrupted Gatsby. He flipped a switch. The grey windows disappeared as the house glowed full of light.
> In the music-room Gatsby turned on a solitary lamp beside the piano. He lit Daisy's cigarette from a trembling match, and sat down with her on a couch far across the room...
> When Klipspringer had played "The Love Nest" he turned around on the bench and searched unhappily for Gatsby in the gloom.
> [more Klipspringer dialogue]
> "Don't talk so much, old sport," commanded Gatsby. "Play!"
> "In the morning, In the evening, Ain't we got fun—"

Draft:
> "I know what we'll do," said Gatsby, "we'll have the piano."
> He called, and presently music drifted up; when it had begun he lit Daisy's cigarette from a trembling match and sat with her far across the room, where there was no light save what the gleaming floor bounced in from the hall.
> "In the morning, in the evening, ain't we got fun—"

The phrase "music drifted up" suggests they are upstairs and music comes from below. But in the source, they go downstairs to the music room. This creates a mild spatial confusion — but a reader would understand: piano music is playing, Gatsby and Daisy sit together in dim light, the song plays. It's not structurally broken; it's just a slightly imprecise compression. The reader is not misled about any fact that matters to the story. Not a valid finding.

After thorough review, I find no sentences in either draft that genuinely fail any of the five structural tests in a way that is not already covered by the authorized cuts.
